nodes.label: Joel Mokyr
nodes.date_label: “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” 1977 · The Lever of Riches 1990 · editor’s introduction, The British Industrial Revolution 1999 · The Gifts of Athena 2002 · Max Weber Lecture on the European Enlightenment 2007 · The Enlightened Economy 2009 · with Kelly and Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” 2014 · A Culture of Growth 2016 · “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” 2023 · with Tabellini, “Why China and Europe Diverged” 2023 · economics prize 2025
nodes.description: An economic historian of technology at Northwestern University who explained sustained growth by the growth of “useful knowledge”. In 1977 he judged demand factors “of a secondary order of importance” in the Industrial Revolution. His 1999 introduction defended the term against the charge that it was “a concept too many” and defined the Industrial Revolution as “a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions”. Two drafts of 2002, which say they adapt The Gifts of Athena (2002; unread here, though its reviewer Zorina Khan reports the same scheme), divided useful knowledge into “propositional” knowledge of natural regularities and “prescriptive” instructions (February), and called the Enlightenment’s contribution “the Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention”, finding Pomeranz’s coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself” unable to explain the gap (October). In a 2007 lecture the Enlightenment kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out”. Reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), C. Knick Harley wondered whether “causation from Enlightenment … to economic change actually existed”, while finding that the book made “a strong case” that “the history of ideas and their place in society needs to be at the core of the story” (2010). In Claude Diebolt’s account of A Culture of Growth (2016), culture works “as the invisible hand”, in a phenomenon “related to an elite” of philosophers, scientists, engineers, instrument makers and industrialists; Diebolt regretted “the lack of in-depth consideration of the German language literature” (2017). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda he answered Robert Allen’s high-wage explanation with British workers’ human capital (2014), and found that across England’s 41 counties industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023). With Guido Tabellini he traced China’s and Europe’s political divergence to clans and corporations (2023). In 2025 he was awarded a share of the economics prize in memory of Alfred Nobel, cited “for having identified the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress”.

nodes.label: E. A. Wrigley
nodes.date_label: Cambridge Group founded (with Laslett) 1964 · with Schofield, The Population History of England 1981 · Ellen McArthur lectures 1987 · Continuity, Chance and Change 1988 · with Davies, Oeppen and Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution 1997 · Poverty, Progress, and Population 2004 · Energy and the English Industrial Revolution 2010 · The Path to Sustained Growth 2016
nodes.description: A historical demographer and economic historian at Cambridge, who founded the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure with Peter Laslett in 1964. With Roger Schofield he reconstructed England’s population from the registers of 404 parishes by “back projection”, making it “possible for the first time” to follow “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981); a family-reconstitution study, a technique perfected by Louis Henry, was its complement (1997). He called the industrial revolution his “first main research interest”, to which he “returned increasingly” after years of population history. In Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), from his 1987 Ellen McArthur lectures, he questioned it as “a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon”: growth came from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time”, as an “organic economy” bounded by the productivity of the land met a new one using mineral energy. Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010) asked “not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end”, without offering energy as the only explanation: there could be “no single, ‘true’ account”, and to downplay institutional and scientific explanations would be “presumptuous and mildly ridiculous”. Mining coal “provided the solution” (2016). He judged Rostow’s “take-off” “now almost impossible to maintain” (2004). Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990). Readers set his energy argument beside Pomeranz’s coal (Mokyr in a draft of 2002, Huang in 2002, Clark and Jacks in 2007), and Wong said that China Transformed had followed his arguments on coal (2016).

nodes.label: Jan de Vries
nodes.date_label: The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis, 1600–1750 1976 · “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” 1994 · with van der Woude, The First Modern Economy 1997 · The Industrious Revolution 2008
nodes.description: An economic historian of the Netherlands and early modern Europe at Berkeley. The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis (1976) studied “the last great epoch before the onset of industrialization”; Pomeranz later called it “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”. His “industrious revolution”, proposed in his Economic History Association presidential address published in 1994, was meant “to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting”: “a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon”. In The Industrious Revolution (2008) he dated it to “roughly 1650–1850”, when households in north-western Europe and British North America reallocated “the time of their members” to earn money and to buy goods. He took the term from Akira Hayami, who had contrasted Japan’s labour-intensive path with Western industrialisation. He built the argument on the revisionist macroeconomics that cut British growth estimates “by more than half”, on the Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, and on Becker’s household economics; against a supply-side orthodoxy he illustrated with Mokyr, he sought to “restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (2008). With Ad van der Woude he presented the Dutch Republic as “the first modern economy” (1997), against historians who saw its achievement as “backward looking”; van Zanden doubted that Dutch growth was much faster than England’s (2002). Pomeranz used the industrious revolution for Chinese households (2000). Reviewers found The Industrious Revolution “on all the main points, convincing” (Voth, 2009), or thought it made consumption a new “deus ex machina” and played down power between the sexes (van Nederveen Meerkerk, 2009). From the history of papermaking, Leonard Rosenband challenged its chronology and mechanism: paperworkers already laboured long hours at the outset of the period, and women and adolescents worked for wages in paper mills long before it (2016).

nodes.label: R. Bin Wong
nodes.date_label: with Will, Nourish the People 1991 · China Transformed 1997 · with Rosenthal, Before and Beyond Divergence 2011 · “Divergence Displaced” 2016
nodes.description: A historian of China at UCLA whose China Transformed (1997) compared Chinese and European economic change, state formation and popular protest without treating Europe as the norm. As Joel Mokyr read it, Wong held that before 1800 Europe and China shared “Smithian expansion, rural industry, population expansion, a growth in consumer demand”, and that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (1997, p. 31, as Mokyr quotes it). Kenneth Pomeranz wrote that he was “following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, while giving “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000). Wong later said that the book had located Europe’s difference in science and technology, “following arguments of E. A. Wrigley” on coal (2016). With Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, in Before and Beyond Divergence (2011), he turned to “political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”: war drew European craft production into cities, so that the question became “why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (his 2016 account); as Debin Ma reported the mechanism, higher urban wages there biased innovation towards saving labour. Ma judged the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” but found this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter” (2012). In “Divergence Displaced” (2016) he judged Brenner’s agrarian social relations, Pomeranz’s coal and colonies and his own earlier book alike open to “non-falsifiability”. Mokyr had objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft).

edges.relationship: Useful knowledge and the epistemic base of technique: propositional and prescriptive knowledge, macro- and microinventions, and stasis where techniques rest on “narrow epistemic bases” (1999, 2002)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. Editor’s introduction (1999, author-posted manuscript): “a successful macroinvention meets three criteria: novelty, workability, and potential for further improvement” (p. 14); “A technological definition of the Industrial Revolution is a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions” (p. 16). “Useful Knowledge as an Evolving System” (draft revised February 2002, pp. 2–7): “in the past centuries useful knowledge has become a dominant factor in History” (p. 2); useful knowledge is partitioned into “propositional” knowledge, which “describes and catalogues natural phenomena and the relationships between them”, and “prescriptive” knowledge, “instructions that can be executed” (p. 5); “Inventions based on narrow epistemic bases have low adaptability and tend to lead to technological stasis fairly soon after their emergence” (p. 7). The draft says it adapts The Gifts of Athena (2002), which is unread; Khan’s review of that book (EH.Net, 2003, read in full) reports the same two categories and quotes it (p. 16): “so many scholars believe that if incentives and demand are right, somehow technology will follow automatically”. The Royal Swedish Academy’s 2025 press release (read) summarises the claim: “we not only need to know that something works, but we also need to have scientific explanations for why.” The 1999 distinction of invention from adoption is the existing strand technology/invention_adoption; this arrow adds the 2002 theory of knowledge. Its use to explain Britain’s Industrial Revolution is drawn on the debate arrow (edge_1086).

edges.relationship: Coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job”: the gap needed “a better explanation than historical luck … or geographical accident”, and Pomeranz did not confront the Needham questions (2002)
edges.evidence_note: “The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, author’s draft of October 2002 for the Riverside conference of November 2002 (pp. 2–4 read; draft pagination). Of coal: “Without denigrating the importance of coal or steam, the argument can be and has been overdone” (p. 2); “China’s coal reserves are immense” (p. 3). Of ghost acreage: “this argument is not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job” (p. 3). Pomeranz “does not confront the ‘Needham Questions’ squarely” (p. 4); “the sheer enormity of the gap requires a better explanation than historical luck (European discoveries) or geographical accident (coal, proximity to America)” (p. 4). The alternative he offers is the Industrial Enlightenment (p. 10), drawn on joel_mokyr → capitalismdebates (edge_1086). A draft (“little more than notes”, its title page says); no published version was read. Revision 1.146 moves this critique from edge_1050 (capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz), where revision 1.145 listed Mokyr among five named critics, to its own arrow; edge_1050 no longer names him.

edges.relationship: Reconstructing England’s population from parish registers: with Schofield, 404 parishes and “back projection” to trace “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981), complemented by family reconstitution (1997), in the Cambridge Group he co-founded (1964)
edges.evidence_note: Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981; introduction pp. 1–5 read in the publisher excerpt of the 1989 Cambridge paperback, OCRed): “since pre-industrial societies normally experienced great difficulty in achieving a rapid expansion in their capacity to produce goods and services, population was the more dynamic element in the striking of a balance with production” (p. 1); the registers make it “possible for the first time to establish with some precision what changes took place in a pre-industrial population over a period of time long enough to encompass a secular cycle of population development, and to investigate the relationship between demographic and economic change during its course” (p. 2); monthly totals “taken from the registers of a total of 404 parishes” (p. 3); “the technique of back projection, which was developed to make the best use of the aggregative data assembled” (p. 4); the aggregative tabulations began as “a subsidiary element” of the Cambridge Group’s family-reconstitution work of “the middle 1960s” (p. 5). Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997, pp. 3–4, read): “This book is intended as a complement to the Population history of England”; family reconstitution “had then recently been perfected by Louis Henry”. The Cambridge Group’s institutional history (read) dates its founding by Laslett and Wrigley to 1964. A collaborative project: Schofield, Oeppen and Davies share these results, and the reconstruction’s estimates are not adjudicated here. edges.relationship: Technologies to exploit coal as Europe’s difference: China Transformed (1997) followed “arguments of E. A. Wrigley”, as Wong recalled in 2016

A. Wrigley, the importance of technologies to exploit coal as a source of energy to power new kinds of machines”; his note cites Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Qualification: this is Wong’s retrospective account. China Transformed is read only in chapter openings, and the passage that cites Wrigley there was not read. edges.relationship: Coal in explanations of British industrialisation, as readers compare them: Mokyr places Pomeranz in a tradition “established by … E.A. Wrigley” (2002); Huang says Pomeranz simplified “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument” (2002); Clark and Jacks find that both “have made coal central to the story” (2007)
edges.evidence_note: Readers’ comparisons, read. Mokyr (October 2002 draft, p. 2): Pomeranz’s coal argument “joins a venerable tradition established by Carlo Cipolla, E.A. Wrigley and others that looks at the Industrial Revolution as primarily a revolution of fossil fuel usage”. Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 532–533, read in revision 1.144): Wrigley (1988) is “a very different thing from arguing that chance, or coal, alone mattered”; Pomeranz has turned “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument that chance figured in England’s industrialization into a simple argument that coal and colonies alone mattered.” Clark and Jacks (European Review of Economic History 2007, abstract): “both E. A. Wrigley and Kenneth Pomeranz have made coal central to the story”; their coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England’s possession of coal reserves. A comparison, not an influence: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read (the read pages of The Great Divergence cite Wrigley only on England’s early divergence from the continent, p. 6 n. 8). Wrigley’s argument stresses chance and the end of the organic economy; Pomeranz pairs coal with colonies.

edges.relationship: The “industrious revolution” applied to Chinese household labour (2000), and de Vries’s 1976 book cited as “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000; later-edition preview, read): labour deployment in Chinese families “seems to closely resemble the reorientation of labor, leisure, and consumption toward the market that Jan DeVries has called Europe’s ‘industrious revolution’” (p. 17; n. 28 cites DeVries 1994b); the contents list a section “Family Labor in China and Europe: ‘Involution’ and the ‘Industrious Revolution’”; “A good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis is DeVries 1976” (p. 3 n. 2). Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 520–521, read in revision 1.144) reads the borrowing critically: “it is surprising that Pomeranz would have tried to equate the Yangzi delta with de Vries’ industrious revolution”, “along the same lines as R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”; “he tries to take the revolution out of de Vries’ industrious revolution.” The use is Pomeranz’s; de Vries’s own later judgement of The Great Divergence (Historically Speaking, 2011) is unread and not drawn. The Huang–Pomeranz dispute over involution is on edges 1043–1044.

edges.relationship: With van der Woude, the Dutch Republic as “the first modern economy”, 1500–1815, against readings of its achievement as “backward looking”, joining Annales structural history to the New Economic History (1997); van Zanden doubted that Dutch growth was much faster than England’s (2002)
edges.evidence_note: De Vries and van der Woude, The First Modern Economy (1997, chapter 1, pp. 1–5 read in the publisher excerpt, OCRed): historians including Hobsbawm, Braudel and Wallerstein “felt certain that the Dutch achievement was essentially backward looking, the culmination of something with no future” (p. 1); they quote North and Thomas, for whom the Netherlands was “the first country to achieve sustained economic growth” (p. 2); “With this work we accept the challenge of the modern historical schools; indeed, we even seek to integrate them”: the Annales school, which “advocated a break with ‘event-centered history’”, and cliometrics, which “shifted the focus of the literature from politics and institutions to markets and rational decision makers” (p. 4); “This book, in short, presents the history of the first modern economy” (p. 4). Van Zanden (EHR 2002, abstract, read): “economic growth in the Netherlands was probably not much faster than in England, as is clear from the development of real wages”, and its modernity “appears to be a product of economic and institutional changes in the middle ages.” The book’s sectoral and analytical chapters are unread; the claim is the co-authors’ framing. De Vries’s criticism of the “backward looking” reading is recorded here, not as arrows to Braudel or Hobsbawm, because one paragraph groups them with Barbour and Wallerstein.

edges.relationship: The Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, with Hajnal’s marriage pattern, as one of the literatures that “guided my thinking” (2008)
edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, p. 8, publisher excerpt, read): among four “modern developments in history and economics” that “have guided my thinking”, “3. The Western European Marriage Pattern. The pioneering work of ‘The Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure’ established the view that the nuclear family structures of modern western European countries and their offshoots are not a product of industrialization but have much earlier origins”, with “the seminal articles of John Hajnal”; “its distinctive economic behavior remains an open question.” The 1994 article’s reference list (Cambridge Core, metadata) cites Wrigley and Schofield (1981), Laslett (1965, 1977) and Hajnal (1965). The influence is credited to the Cambridge Group and Hajnal, not to Wrigley alone; demography/john_hajnal already records Hajnal as a resource for de Vries.

edges.relationship: Demand restored against the supply-side orthodoxy, which de Vries illustrates with Mokyr’s view that the Industrial Revolution’s “when,” “where” and “how fast” are “to be sought first and foremost in supply” (1977; 2008)
edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, pp. 6–7, publisher excerpt, read): “Studies of modern economic growth are inevitably founded on a decisive ‘supply-side’ advance”; Adam Smith left no doubt that “The consumer responds to the developing productive forces, not the other way around”, with n. 17 quoting Mokyr’s “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” (JEH 1977, p. 1005): “The determination of ‘when,’ ‘where,’ and ‘how fast’ are to be sought first and foremost in supply, not demand-related processes”; “What began as an effort to restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (p. 7). Mokyr’s 1977 abstract (Cambridge Core, read): demand factors “were definitely of a secondary order of importance”. The 1994 article’s reference list cites the 1977 article. Qualification: de Vries cites Mokyr as an exemplar of a general orthodoxy; this is not a reply to a Mokyr text on the industrious revolution, and no reply by Mokyr was read.

edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison of China’s and Europe’s advanced regions: Pomeranz followed “a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000)
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000, pp. 7–8, later-edition preview, read): a regional approach “anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong” (p. 7); “Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as ‘deviations’ when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm” (p. 8); “my concrete application of this reciprocal comparative method has some significant differences from Wong’s”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures and reciprocal influences” (p. 8 and n. 13). Readers: Parthasarathi (2011, p. 5): “Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work”; Huang (2002, p. 520) traces Pomeranz’s use of the industrious revolution to “R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”. Wong (Comparativ 2016, read): Pomeranz rejected “numerous putative differences … including my China Transformed” (p. 73); China Transformed “followed the same method” (p. 76); both books “shared … the basic problem of non-falsifiability” (p. 77). The same debt is recorded as the strand global/reciprocal_comparison_resources (carried by edge_898); this arrow makes it a relationship between the two entries.

edges.relationship: From the limits of European experience to political scale: with Rosenthal, Wong argued that European fragmentation and warfare concentrated manufacturing in cities, where higher wage costs favoured labour-saving techniques (2011, as Wong summarised in 2016 and Ma reported in 2012); in 2016 he recast divergence from “why Britain” to a more general transformation
edges.evidence_note: His own words, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, pp. 77–78, read): “Rosenthal and I ended up focusing on an important political difference between China and Europe – political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”; war gave “craft producers an incentive to locate in cities”; “We turned the issue of divergence from a question of why was Britain the first industrializer to why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (p. 77); “By making the question of the great divergence a more general one we recognize that even a profoundly transformative process like modern economic growth could take place in several ways and begin at several locations” (p. 78). Before and Beyond Divergence (2011) is unread; Ma’s review (EH.Net 2012, read in full in revision 1.145) reports the same dichotomy of “a unified and centralized imperial China versus a politically fragmented Europe” and the mechanism: warfare brought “a greater degree of concentration of trade and manufacturing in urban locations”, and, “With higher urban wages”, innovation in Europe “would be more biased towards saving labor than in China”. Ma finds this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter”, and the evidence on public goods “even shakier”. He also reports the authors’ challenge to “the accepted thesis of China being a high interest rate and capital scarce country”, and judges the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” for addressing “some of the key issues beyond what has been done recently by Pomeranz, Allen and others”, though “far less so when it comes to providing credible support for its own thesis”. The wage mechanism is Ma’s report; Wong’s 2016 summary gives the move of craft production to cities. Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014, p. 16.2) say Rosenthal and Wong “adopted” Allen’s induced-innovation argument “wholesale”. China Transformed (1997), as Mokyr quotes it, held that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (p. 31); Mokyr objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft, pp. 3–4). The co-authored argument is Rosenthal’s as well as Wong’s.

edges.relationship: Brenner’s agrarian social relations, like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, are traits particular to Britain, so that their necessity “cannot be falsified” (2016)
edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 2016, pp. 74–75, read): “when my colleague and Marxist historian Robert Brenner famously argues that it is the absence of the agrarian social relations found in Britain that prevented the emergence of capitalism elsewhere, the importance of the system through which he sees the modern world economy emerging cannot be falsified because the enclosures and the social relations that attended them were particular to Britain. Like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, Brenner cites traits that are British and not present elsewhere” (p. 74); “Neither the scientific revolution nor agrarian social relations lend themselves very easily to counterfactual exercises because they are themselves so large and encompassing” (p. 75). He allows that such traits “could in fact be factors helping to explain the industrial revolution” (p. 75). A methodological critique in one passage, citing the Aston and Philpin collection; it does not dispute Brenner’s evidence. Brenner’s other respondents are on capitalismdebates → robert_brenner (edge_1078), which does not name Wong.

Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Vries ('A World of Surprising Resemblances?', 2009, pp. 35–38, 47–48 read), on agriculture and the state: 'I would not call that a "surprising resemblance"' (p. 38); 'Coal and colonies definitely were fundamental in the Rise of the West. But reference to them cannot suffice to explain it' (p. 48). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: 'our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England'; 'Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism' (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the 'rise of the west' literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: 'The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers' (p. 958); the qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates, and moved Brenner and Isett's 2002 critique to its own arrow (robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz), as this note had foreseen. Revision 1.146 likewise moved Mokyr's 2002 critique to its own arrow (joel_mokyr → kenneth_pomeranz), since Mokyr became a person entry; the four interventions above remain.

edge_1086.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause of sustained growth: the “Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention” (2002 draft), which kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out” (2007 lecture); with Kelly and Ó Gráda, British workers’ human capital against Allen’s high-wage explanation (2014), and low initial wages and mechanical skills across England’s 41 counties (2023)
edge_1086.evidence_note: His own words, read. October 2002 draft (“The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, p. 10): Enlightenment thinkers “created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention.” Max Weber Lecture (EUI, 2007, pp. 2–5): countries of the 1914 “convergence club” “were countries that in the eighteenth century were subject to the European Enlightenment. This strong correlation is not in and of itself proof of causality” (p. 2); the tightening of propositional and prescriptive knowledge “prevented the early Industrial Revolution from fizzling out and enabled it to become the taproot of modern growth” (p. 5). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.2–16.4): “the main reason for its precocity was its higher level of human capital”; against Allen’s induced innovation, “the driver of technological progress was something deeper and stronger than cheap coal and high wages”. “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (JPE 2023, pp. 60–61): their prediction “runs directly counter to the influential argument of Allen (2009a)”; the finding concerns the 41 counties of England, not Britain’s international position. The Enlightened Economy (2009) is unread; reviewing it, Harley (EH.Net, 2010, read) wondered “if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed” and found that it “seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.” Each quotation is tied to the text it comes from; the 2002 wording is not claimed for the 2009 book. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from technology because Mokyr had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to joel_mokyr and keeps its id. His theory of useful knowledge as such is drawn on joel_mokyr → technology.

edge_1084.relationship: The Industrial Revolution as escape from an “organic economy” bounded by land: growth from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (1988), the question “why it did not come to an end”, without dismissing institutional or scientific explanations (2010), and coal as “the solution” (2016); Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990)
edge_1084.evidence_note: His own words, in Cambridge University Press excerpts. Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8 read in revision 1.145): “After many years spent in work principally concerned with the population history of England, I had returned increasingly to my first main research interest, the better understanding of the industrial revolution” (p. 1); “My main aim in the lectures was to question the appropriateness of the view that the industrial revolution was a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon” (p. 3); growth was “the product of two different sets of forces having only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (p. 4); the classical economists remain authoritative for “an economy bounded by the productivity of the land, what I shall term an organic economy” (p. 5). Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11 read): “the most important single issue on which to focus in trying to gain a clearer understanding of the industrial revolution is not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end” (p. 4); “the production horizon for all organic economies was set by the annual cycle of plant growth” (p. 9); “There can be no single, ‘true’ account of the industrial revolution” (p. 4); institutional and scientific explanations get “only glancing references”, but “it would be both presumptuous and mildly ridiculous to downplay their importance”, and the explanations are “essentially incommensurable” (pp. 4–5). The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, p. 3): “Mining coal provided the solution to this problem.” Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004, pp. 1–3): Rostow’s “take-off” is “now almost impossible to maintain” (p. 2), and Berg and Hudson put the counter-view “vigorously and effectively” (p. 3 n. 6). The 2013 article is read in abstract only. Critique: Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper, read): “The work of Wrigley and Schofield dominates the population history of this period and illustrates some of the more general problems of causal analysis based on aggregative studies.” Their objection concerns causal inference from the aggregate series, not the reconstruction as such. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from demography because Wrigley had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to e_a_wrigley and keeps its id. His population reconstruction is drawn on e_a_wrigley → demography.

edge_1085.relationship: The “industrious revolution”: a household-level, demand-side change that preceded the supply-side Industrial Revolution (1994), built on the revision that cut British growth estimates “by more than half” and dated to roughly 1650–1850 (2008); reviewers asked whether consumption had become a new “deus ex machina” (2009), and papermaking evidence challenged its chronology and mechanism (2016)
edge_1085.evidence_note: His own words, read. JEH 1994, abstract (Cambridge Core): “The Industrial Revolution as a historical concept has many shortcomings. A new concept—the ‘industrious revolution’—is proposed to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting … The industrious revolution was a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon.” The Industrious Revolution (2008, publisher excerpt, pp. 6–10): “the accumulating evidence for an earlier increase of per capita income in northwestern Europe paired with a major refinement of material life casts serious doubt on the orthodoxy that the Industrial Revolution was the actual starting point for long-term economic growth” (pp. 6–7); among the literatures that “guided my thinking” is “The Revisionist Macroeconomics of the British Industrial Revolution”, which “reduces the earlier growth estimates by more than half” (pp. 7–8, citing Crafts and Harley 1992); the approach would “question the claims of the twin revolutions – the British Industrial and the French political – to function as gatekeepers to modern history” (p. 9); households “acted to reallocate their productive resources (which are chiefly the time of their members)” during “a long eighteenth century, roughly 1650–1850” (p. 10). Reviewers, read: Voth (EH.Net, 2009) finds the book “on all the main points, convincing”, with “the almost complete disconnect with behavioral economics” as its weakness; van Nederveen Meerkerk (TSEG, 2009) finds that consumption becomes “een nieuwe ‘deus ex machina’” (p. 176). Rosenband (2016, abstract): papermaking raises “fundamental challenges to this model”; “paperworkers already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness”, and “women and adolescent workers toiled for wages in paper mills long before the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries”. The 1994 article’s pages read in earlier revisions are not quoted here. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from consumption because de Vries had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to jan_de_vries and keeps its id. Pomeranz’s use of the concept is now on jan_de_vries → kenneth_pomeranz; the household mechanism stays on consumption/household_labor.

rationale: The 1.145 debate entry left Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong as roster rows and drew their component contributions from fields “for now”. Each now has at least three edges and at least eight dated points. Mokyr, Wrigley and de Vries each have at least three points read in their own words. Wong has two independently read texts in his own words (the chapter openings of China Transformed and “Divergence Displaced”, 2016); his 2011 point rests on his own 2016 summary and Ma’s review. Every person therefore meets the rule of at least two edges and three timeline points backed by read evidence. Every edge rests on a text read in the person’s own words (author-posted papers, publisher excerpts, Cambridge Core openings and abstracts, an open-access article) or on a named reader’s explicit statement; unread books (The Gifts of Athena, The Enlightened Economy, A Culture of Growth, Before and Beyond Divergence) are given only through named reviewers or their authors’ later summaries. Source links are official: DOIs, publisher pages and excerpts, the authors’ own postings and open-access journal or repository copies. The new jan_de_vries entry and the revised edge_1085 quote de Vries (1994) only from its publisher abstract; previously accepted page-based claims from that article remain. The Mokyr 1999 essay was re-read in his own posted copy. Nothing is drawn twice: edges 1084–1086 change source rather than gaining twins, and Mokyr’s critique of Pomeranz leaves edge_1050. Weak or thin links are left out (see each draft’s edges_considered_not_proposed).
